outcome: No existence or nonexistence result has appeared since 26 January 2024: every source read still treats the question as open. The only post-freeze item on the problem, a 12 January 2026 Lean 4 formalization, restates the question as open and formalizes an empirical search statement, with no new mathematics on existence.
problem_asks: One existence question: whether there exist positive integers m and n with gcd(m,n)=1 such that the sum of the proper divisors of m equals n and the sum of the proper divisors of n equals m (a relatively prime amicable pair). An affirmative answer requires exhibiting such a pair; a negative answer requires a proof that none exists. The statement asks for no bound, count or case split.

events.what_happened: Chen, Tang and Zhan posted arXiv:2601.07444, 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', a Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of amicable-number theory (Thabit ibn Qurra's rule, Euler's generalization, the Borho-Hoffmann breeding method, sociable and betrothed numbers). Section 2.3 states that all known amicable pairs have gcd(m,n) > 1 and that whether coprime amicable pairs exist is an open problem. Section 3.7.5 formalizes the empirical observation that no coprime amicable pair has been found below a bound: 'if a coprime amicable pair exists, the product of its members must exceed' 10^65, which the paper calls 'a statement of empirical fact from computation, not a mathematical theorem'. Table 2 lists a 'No coprime amicable pairs conjecture' as a Lean definition, and Section 3.8 formalizes three open problems as definitions, not proofs.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page (no later versions listed).
events.delivers: No existence or nonexistence fact about coprime amicable pairs. Its only quantitative content on the question is the restated empirical bound: any coprime pair would have product above 10^65, a claim the paper attributes to older computation and does not itself carry out. Its Lean results concern the general theory of amicable pairs (Thabit rule, Borho-Hoffmann method), not coprimality.
events.remains: The whole problem: whether any coprime amicable pair exists, and whether none does.
events.time_since_posted: about 9 months (posted 12 January 2026; this record dated 11 October 2026)

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib v4.15.0 (per the repository README)
machine_checked.note: The paper's Code Availability section states zero sorry placeholders and complete proofs of all major theorems. I did not read the Lean files. The README I read says the general Thabit rule is still to be proved, which contradicts the paper (see doubts). The paper uses native_decide (Section 3.3), which trusts compiled code rather than the kernel alone.

events.doubts: (1) Conflict on the general Thabit rule. The paper says 'A key contribution of this work is the complete formal proof of the Thabit ibn Qurra formula' and lists thabit_rule_general for all k >= 1 (Section 3.6, Table 3). The repository README (read through the GitHub page, Contributing section) says 'Prove the general Thabit rule for all n (currently verified for n=2,4)'. The repository has 2 commits and I could not see a last-commit date. I could not resolve which is current; the raw README URL returned 404. (2) Provenance of the 10^65 statement. The introduction cites it to reference [7], given as Paul Pollack, 'On relatively prime amicable pairs', Colloquium Mathematicum, 2015. Section 3.7.5 says the product bound is 'Based on work by Pedersen (2003) and others', and Pedersen does not appear in the reference list. Suzuki (2018) cites a different Pollack 2015 paper (Moscow J. Combin. Number Theory 5 (2015) 36-51) for an explicit bound. I did not find the paper under the Lean paper's title, and the search that produced the 10^65 figure is not described. (3) The formalization turns this bound into a Lean definition-level statement; it adds nothing to the existence question itself.
events.direction: Neutral on existence. It states the question is open, formalizes 'no coprime amicable pairs exist' as a Lean definition, and formalizes an empirical search bound. It cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: Mavaddat and Alikhani, 'Amicable numbers and their connection to the Euler totient function' (arXiv:2512.22319, math.HO, 13 pages). It characterizes amicable pairs whose gcd is a power of two, through three configurations: A = 2^n·ab with B = 2^n·cd (Theorem 2.1); A = 2^n·abc with B = 2^n·de (Theorem 2.3); A = 2^n·abc with B = 2^n·def (Theorem 2.5), each with an identity relating phi(A)+phi(B) to the odd prime factors.
events.delivers: Restricted to the three configurations above, all carrying a 2^n factor. The statement gives no range for n. The proofs use phi(2^n) = 2^(n-1), which needs n >= 1, so for n >= 1 both members are even and the coprime case (gcd 1, n = 0) is outside these theorems. The paper neither states nor treats the coprime case. It says nothing about whether coprime amicable pairs exist.
events.remains: All of the problem. Whether the 2-power-gcd analysis could be extended to gcd 1 is not established by the text I read.
events.direction: Neutral on existence. It concerns amicable pairs with a 2-power gcd, which for n >= 1 are both even, so it lies outside the coprime case.

Proposes new generalizations of amicable numbers (multiamicable k-tuples with weighted sums, as described in OEIS A383239 and A385492) and proves properties of them. Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), article 25.4.2, per a search snippet (journal page not opened).

events.what_happened: Bishop, Bozarth, Kuss and Peet, 'The Abundancy Index and Feebly Amicable Numbers' (arXiv:2104.11366). Defines feebly amicable (harmonious) pairs m, n with n/sigma(n) + m/sigma(m) = 1, tests whether every number has one, and offers questions and conjectures. events.what_happened: Yuta Suzuki, 'On amicable tuples' (arXiv:1711.06847, submitted 18 Nov 2017; Illinois J. Math. 62 (2018) 225-252; received 31 Jan 2018, revised 16 Jul 2018). Improves Pollack's bound: for relatively prime amicable pairs (M,N) with K = omega(MN) distinct prime factors, MN < (pi^2/6)·2^(4^K - 2·2^K); extends to some amicable tuples. The abstract presents Gmelin's 1917 nonexistence claim as a conjecture.
events.revisions: One arXiv version (v1). Journal version Illinois J. Math. 62 (2018) 225-252.
events.delivers: For each fixed K, an explicit bound on the product of any coprime amicable pair with K distinct prime factors in MN. It is conditional on such a pair existing, so it says nothing about existence, and it does not bound K.
events.remains: Existence for every K, including pairs with unboundedly many prime factors; and whether any coprime pair exists at all.

events.what_happened: Gmelin (1917) noted that none of the amicable pairs then known had relatively prime members and conjectured that no relatively prime amicable pair exists. The original publication was not located; the attribution comes from Suzuki (2018) and secondary summaries.
events.delivers: A conjecture, not a result. It states the nonexistence answer to the question, supported only by the then-known pairs.
events.doubts: The conjecture was made on the basis of the pairs known in 1917; its support has since been changed by the discovery of very many pairs, all of which share a prime factor, and no coprime pair among them.
events.direction: Conjectures the negative answer: no relatively prime amicable pair exists.

events.what_happened: Hagis, 'On relatively prime odd amicable numbers', Mathematics of Computation 23 (1969), no. 107, 539-543 (MR 0246816; DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1969-0246816-7). Per the AMS listing's abstract as shown in a search snippet, it derives necessary conditions for an odd relatively prime amicable pair: lower bounds on m, n, mn and on the number of prime divisors of mn, using a large computation. The AMS page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch, so this comes from the search snippet.
events.delivers: Necessary conditions for odd coprime pairs, which hold if such a pair exists. Restricted to odd pairs. It makes no existence claim.

disputes.summary: Pollack's 2015 paper: Suzuki (2018) cites Moscow J. Combin. Number Theory 5 (2015) 36-51 for an explicit bound on coprime amicable pairs; the January 2026 Lean paper cites 'Pollack, On relatively prime amicable pairs, Colloquium Mathematicum, 2015' as the source of the 10^65 search statement. I did not find the paper under either description, so this is unresolved.

Source of the 10^65 search statement: the Lean paper's introduction cites reference [7] (Pollack), while Section 3.7.5 says 'Based on work by Pedersen (2003) and others', and Pedersen is not in the reference list. The Pedersen-García-te Riele survey was not read.

Status of the general Thabit rule: the Lean paper says the complete formal proof of the Thabit formula, thabit_rule_general for all k >= 1, is a key contribution; the repository README says proving the general rule is still future work (verified for n=2,4). Not resolved from what I could read.
Wells's edition year: ProofWiki lists 1986 and 1997 editions; the Wikipedia reference list gives Wells (1987, Penguin) pp. 145-147. The 10^67 statement is the same in both.

summary: I ran 39 web searches and opened the primary sources I could reach for the question whether a relatively prime amicable pair exists. Every source I read treats it as open. The current Wikipedia list (read in October 2026) carries it under Number theory > General, next to the opposite-parity and infinitude questions. ProofWiki's 'Existence of Coprime Amicable Pair' sits in its open-questions category. Suzuki (2018) and the January 2026 Lean paper both state it as unresolved. The literature from 1917 to 2018 (Gmelin's conjecture; Artjuhov 1975 and Borho 1974 finiteness for each fixed K; Pollack 2015; Suzuki 2018; Hagis 1969 and 1970; Yamada 2016; Wells's 10^67 size bound) gives conditional constraints, namely that any such pair would be very large and have many prime factors, but each presupposes existence and none decides it. Since 26 January 2024 I found one item on the problem itself and two neighbouring items. The item on the problem is the Chen-Tang-Zhan Lean formalization (12 January 2026). It restates the question as open, formalizes it as a Lean definition, and formalizes an empirical 10^65 search statement that it attributes to older work and calls 'empirical fact from computation, not a mathematical theorem'. The neighbours are the Mavaddat-Alikhani gcd-power-of-two paper (26 December 2025), whose theorems carry a 2^n factor and so leave the coprime case outside them, and Dimitrov's generalization paper (August 2024), a different notion. Close call: the 10^65 statement could be read as a quantity named in the problem having moved, since it is the largest explicit restriction on a coprime pair I found. I did not record it as a move, because it is not new mathematics, it is attributed to older work whose source I could not confirm, it is an empirical statement, and it is conditional on a pair existing. The Lean paper's claim of a complete general Thabit rule conflicts with its repository README, which I could not resolve from what I read. AI search: I ran explicit searches for AI, LLM, GPT-5, Claude Opus, Gemini Deep Think, AlphaEvolve, Harmonic's Aristotle, DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, Erdos-problem trackers, AI-generated proofs and AI counterexample searches. None linked an AI system to this problem or to amicable pairs in general. The Lean paper, its repository and the Mavaddat-Alikhani paper name no AI system, and the Lean paper does not say how its code was written. The older papers name none in what I read. No source names a system, so ai.none_found is true for each event. The 2026 AI-and-Erdos results in the search results concern other problems. Erdos problem 830 uses a different definition (sigma(a) = sigma(b) = a + b) and is not this question.
competing_reading: The strongest case for something having moved is the Lean paper's 10^65 search statement. It is the largest explicit restriction on a coprime pair in the sources, it sits in a machine-checkable artefact, and the paper formalizes it. Against that: the statement is empirical and attributed to older work whose source is unconfirmed, and it is a size constraint on a hypothetical object, so it cannot move existence in either direction. A second reading treats Hagis, Yamada, Suzuki and Pollack as partial results because they constrain every candidate. Against that: each presupposes a pair exists, and none decides whether one does.
what_would_settle_it: (a) An explicit coprime pair (m,n) with gcd 1 and s(m) = n and s(n) = m, which anyone can check by computing proper-divisor sums, or a published proof that none exists. (b) For the 10^65 statement: the search method and range from the Garcia-Pedersen-te Riele 2003 survey or Pollack's 2015 paper, and confirmation of which paper the Lean paper's reference [7] is. (c) For the Lean artefact: a sorry-free build of chainstart/amicable-numbers, its commit history, and whether thabit_rule_general is actually proved. (d) For AI involvement: an acknowledgement in the Lean paper or a later paper naming a tool. None found.

events.credibility_reason: Paper's claim of a complete general Thabit rule conflicts with its repository README; the 10^65 statement is unsourced (Pollack vs Pedersen attribution conflict). Irrelevant to scope: it formalizes the problem as an open definition.

judgement.why: The statement is a single yes/no existence question with no named quantity, so conditional size or prime-count constraints on a hypothetical coprime pair do not move anything the statement asks: the fixed-K finiteness and explicit size bounds (Borho, Artjuhov, Pollack, Suzuki) are scored none, and the lower bounds that rest on large computations ruling out small candidates (Hagis, Yamada, Wells) are scored instances. The one post-snapshot item on the problem itself, the Chen-Tang-Zhan Lean formalization, restates the question as open and formalizes known or empirical material: none. Mavaddat-Alikhani (gcd a power of two with n>=1, so both members are even), Dimitrov (generalized amicability), the feebly amicable paper and Battiato-Borho (each member coprime to 6, not gcd(m,n)=1) concern changed questions: variant.
